facts.statement: Coelurus lived during the Late Jurassic period, specifically between 155 and 152 million years ago.
facts.quote: Coelurus is a genus of coelurosaurian dinosaur from the Late Jurassic period (mid-late Kimmeridgian faunal stage, 155–152 million years ago).

facts.statement: The name Coelurus means "hollow tail" because the animal possessed hollow tail vertebrae.
facts.quote: The name means "hollow tail", referring to its hollow tail vertebrae (Greek κοῖλος, koilos = hollow + οὐρά, oura = tail).

facts.statement: Coelurus was a small, bipedal carnivore with long legs.
facts.quote: It was a small bipedal carnivore with elongate legs.

facts.statement: The only valid species of Coelurus is C. fragilis, which was described by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1879.
facts.quote: Only one species is currently recognized as valid: the type species, C. fragilis, described by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1879.

facts.statement: Coelurus is known from a single partial skeleton discovered in the Morrison Formation of Wyoming, United States.
facts.quote: It is known from one partial skeleton found in the Morrison Formation of Wyoming, United States.

facts.statement: Othniel Charles Marsh named the species Coelurus fragilis after being impressed by the hollow interiors of its thin-walled vertebrae.
facts.quote: Marsh was impressed with the hollow interiors of the thin-walled vertebrae, a characteristic that gave the type species its name: Coelurus fragilis.

facts.statement: When first described, Marsh estimated Coelurus was about the size of a wolf and likely carnivorous.
facts.quote: He thought of his new genus as an "animal about as large as a wolf, and probably carnivorous".

facts.statement: Marsh initially created a second species, C. agilis, based on fused pubic bones he believed belonged to an animal three times larger than C. fragilis.
facts.quote: Marsh elected to place some of the material in a new species, C. agilis, on the strength of a pair of fused pubic bones he thought belonged to an animal three times the size of C. fragilis.

facts.statement: Henry Fairfield Osborn named the genus Ornitholestes in 1903 based on fossils from the Morrison Formation.
facts.quote: In 1903, Henry Fairfield Osborn named a second genus of small theropod from the Morrison Formation, Ornitholestes.

facts.statement: Charles Gilmore concluded in 1920 that the genera Ornitholestes and Coelurus were synonyms.
facts.quote: Ornitholestes became intertwined with Coelurus in 1920, when Charles Gilmore, in his influential study of theropod dinosaurs, concluded that the two were synonyms.

facts.statement: The synonymy between Ornitholestes and Coelurus was not fully resolved until John Ostrom's study in 1980.
facts.quote: This was followed in the literature for decades. The two genera were not formally compared, however, nor was there a full accounting of what actually belonged to Coelurus, until John Ostrom's study in 1980.

facts.statement: John Ostrom revealed that one of the vertebrae Marsh illustrated for C. fragilis was a composite belonging to an unnamed small theropod from a different quarry.
facts.quote: Additionally, he showed that one of the three vertebrae Marsh had illustrated for C. fragilis was actually a composite of two vertebrae, one of which was later shown to come from another quarry and belonged not to Coelurus but to another, unnamed small theropod.

facts.statement: A partial skeleton discovered in Wyoming in 1995 was initially thought to be a large Coelurus but was later identified as the genus Tanycolagreus.
facts.quote: a later discovery (1995) of a partial skeleton in Wyoming was first thought to be a new larger specimen of Coelurus, but further study showed it belonged to a different but related genus, Tanycolagreus.

facts.statement: Only one species, C. fragilis, is currently recognized as valid for the genus Coelurus despite six other species having been named historically.
facts.quote: Only one species of Coelurus, the type species C. fragilis, is still recognized as valid today, although six other species have been named over the years.

facts.statement: The species C. agilis, named by Marsh in 1884, was later found to consist of additional parts of the C. fragilis skeleton.
facts.quote: C. agilis, as discussed, was named by Marsh in 1884 for what turned out to be additional parts of the skeleton of C. fragilis.

facts.statement: Species C. bauri and C. longicollis were transferred by Cope in 1889 to the new genus Coelophysis.
facts.quote: Cope's C. bauri and C. longicollis, named in 1887 from Late Triassic fossils from New Mexico, were transferred by Cope in 1889 to his new genus Coelophysis.

facts.statement: C. daviesi was named in 1888 based on a neck vertebra from the Early Cretaceous of England and was later transferred to the genus Thecocoelurus.
facts.quote: C. daviesi was named by Richard Lydekker in 1888 for Harry Seeley's Thecospondylus daviesi, a neck vertebra from the Early Cretaceous of England, but this species was later transferred to its own genus, Thecocoelurus.

facts.statement: C. gracilis was named in 1888 based on limb remains, but by 1920 only a single claw remained associated with the species.
facts.quote: C. gracilis, another Early Cretaceous species, was also named in 1888. It was coined by Marsh for what seems to be an assortment of limb remains, but Gilmore could only find a single claw when he reviewed the species in 1920.

facts.statement: C. gracilis has been considered a dubious species outside of Coelurus since the 1920s, when it was assigned to the genus Chirostenotes.
facts.quote: This species has been proposed as outside Coelurus since the 1920s (when Gilmore assigned it to Chirostenotes), and has been regarded as a dubious species outside of Coelurus in recent reviews.

facts.statement: During the time Ornitholestes was considered synonymous with Coelurus, its type species was classified as C. hermanni.
facts.quote: Finally, during the period when Ornitholestes was thought to be the same as Coelurus, its type species was recognized as distinct by Steel, as C. hermanni.

facts.statement: The main skeleton of Coelurus is nearly complete and is housed at the Peabody Museum of Natural History.
facts.quote: Coelurus is known from most of the skeleton of a single individual, including numerous vertebrae, partial pelvic and shoulder girdles, and much of the arms and legs, stored at the Peabody Museum of Natural History

facts.statement: The fossils of Coelurus were found at Reed's Quarry 13 in Como Bluff, Wyoming.
facts.quote: The fossils were recovered from Reed's Quarry 13 at Como Bluff, Wyoming.

facts.statement: Two arm bones possibly belonging to Coelurus were found at the Cleveland-Lloyd Dinosaur Quarry in Utah.
facts.quote: Additionally, two arm bones possibly belonging to this genus are known from the Cleveland-Lloyd Dinosaur Quarry in Utah.

facts.statement: Coelurus weighed between 13 and 20 kilograms, measured about 2.4 meters long, and stood 0.7 meters tall at the hip.
facts.quote: Its weight has been estimated at around 13 to 20 kg, with a length of about 2.4 meters (7.9 ft) and a hip height of 0.7 meters (2.3 ft).

facts.statement: Reconstructions show Coelurus had a long neck and torso, long slender hindlimbs, and a potentially small, slender skull.
facts.quote: From reconstructions of the skeleton, Coelurus had a relatively long neck and torso due to its long vertebrae, a long slender hindlimb due to its long metatarsus, and potentially a small slender skull.

facts.statement: The upper arm bone of Coelurus had an S-shaped curve and was slightly longer than the forearm, measuring 11.9 centimeters compared to 9.6 centimeters.
facts.quote: The upper arm had a distinct S-shaped curve in side view and was slightly longer than the forearm (11.9 centimeters [4.7 in] versus 9.6 centimeters [3.8 in]).

facts.statement: Coelurus possessed a semilunate carpal in its wrist similar to Deinonychus and had long, slender fingers.
facts.quote: The wrist had a semilunate carpal similar to that of Deinonychus, and the fingers were long and slender.

facts.statement: The metatarsals of Coelurus were unusually long and slender, nearly as long as the thigh bones, which measure about 21 centimeters.
facts.quote: The metatarsals were unusually long and slender, nearly the length of the thigh bones (the best preserved thigh bone is about 21 centimeters long [8.3 in]).

facts.statement: Coelurus is distinguished from Ornitholestes by having a longer back and neck, as well as longer and more slender legs and feet.
facts.quote: Coelurus had a longer back and neck than Ornitholestes, and longer, more slender legs and feet.

facts.statement: Coelurus was a small terrestrial carnivore that fed on small prey such as insects, mammals, and lizards.
facts.quote: Coelurus is regarded as a small terrestrial carnivore, feeding on small prey items like insects, mammals, and lizards.

facts.statement: Since the 1980s, Coelurus has generally been classified as a coelurosaurian with uncertain affinities that does not fit well into better-known Cretaceous clades.
facts.quote: Since the growth of phylogenetic studies in the 1980s, Coelurus has usually been found to be a coelurosaurian of uncertain affinities, not fitting with the better-known clades of the Cretaceous.

facts.statement: Coelurus is sometimes placed in its own family, Coeluridae, though the membership of this family has been unstable.
facts.quote: Coelurus is sometimes put into its own family, Coeluridae, although the membership of the family has not been stable.

facts.statement: A 2025 study by Delcourt et al. recovered Coelurus and Nqwebasaurus as the most basal members of Ornithomimosauria based on phylogenetic analyses.
facts.quote: In their comprehensive revision of Santanaraptor and Mirischia, Delcourt et al. (2025) recovered Coelurus and Nqwebasaurus as the basalmost members of Ornithomimosauria based on both equal and implied weight phylogenetic analyses.
